question: When does full-batch gradient flow on a wide neural network have a power-law population training-loss tail, and can the exponent be predicted from the neural tangent kernel's diagonal singularity, input dimension, and regularity of the initial output error?

key_findings.claim: The paper's central result is a conditional spectral identity: power-law kernel eigenvalues and power-law target-tail energy imply a power-law loss trajectory.
key_findings.evidence: For the fixed symmetric evolution operator, the source writes L(t)=one half times sum_n exp(-2 lambda_n t)|c_n|^2. If lambda_n is asymptotic to Lambda n^(-nu) and the coefficient tail s_n=sum_{k>=n}|c_k|^2 is asymptotic to K n^(-kappa), then L(t) is asymptotic to (K/2) Gamma(kappa/nu+1)(2 Lambda t)^(-kappa/nu). Supplementary Theorem 1 proves this implication by summation by parts and integral asymptotics. The theorem does not itself prove that a particular network and target have the two required spectral tails.

key_findings.claim: For a shallow biased ReLU NTK on a smooth full-dimensional density, the leading diagonal singularity has degree one and produces eigenvalue exponent nu=1+1/d.
key_findings.evidence: Expanding the ReLU covariance and NTK around coincident inputs gives a degree-three covariance singularity and a degree-one NTK singularity. Applying the cited singular-integral Weyl law gives lambda_n proportional to n^(-(1+1/d)) and an explicit coefficient Lambda. The derivation requires nonzero bias so the angular map is regular away from the diagonal, and it assumes the density and domain conditions needed by the integral-operator asymptotic.

key_findings.claim: The two advertised ReLU loss exponents apply to narrowly specified initial-error classes, not to arbitrary targets.
key_findings.evidence: For an initial error with a jump across a smooth boundary, the source obtains kappa=1/d and xi=1/(d+1). For a Gaussian-process initial error whose covariance has singularity degree beta=3, it obtains kappa=3/d and xi=3/(d+1). These are assumptions about g(x)=mu(x)^(1/2)(f_initial(x)-f_target(x)), not automatically properties of the target alone. The indicator example is still squared-loss regression on an indicator, not cross-entropy classification.

key_findings.claim: The word universal must be read within a specific population, fixed-kernel, singular-integral asymptotic class.
key_findings.evidence: The analysis starts from expected quadratic loss over a continuous smooth density, linearizes near a zero-loss global optimum, and freezes the kernel. It excludes ordinary minibatch noise, finite-data sampling, cross-entropy, regularization, momentum, adaptive optimizers, and feature-learning trajectories unless separately justified. The derived exponent is universal only after the kernel singularity degree and initial-error roughness class are fixed.

key_findings.claim: On a fixed finite dataset, the ultimate linearized loss is not generically an eternal power law.
key_findings.evidence: A finite M-by-M positive kernel matrix has only finitely many eigenvalues, so continuous-time loss ultimately decays at the smallest positive eigenvalue's exponential rate, or retains a nullspace plateau. The paper instead treats M as large enough to approximate a continuous density before taking large time. Figure 1 visibly bends at the finite-spectrum tail. Therefore the data-to-continuum limit must precede the t-to-infinity limit for the claimed asymptotic.

anchors.section: Figure 1 / finite M spectra and trajectories

key_findings.claim: Most numerical evidence diagonalizes an analytically constructed infinite-width kernel rather than training a neural network.
key_findings.evidence: Supplement A distinguishes two experiment types. The main type forms the infinite-width NTK on about 10,000 sampled inputs, stores the dense matrix, diagonalizes it at cubic cost, and reconstructs loss spectrally. Actual networks appear only in selected panels, typically width 3,000; the GP target itself is generated by a width-one-million network. This supports the kernel calculation much more directly than it validates finite-width neural optimization.

key_findings.claim: The finite-network tests are too underspecified to establish optimizer-robust scaling.
key_findings.evidence: The source says the discrete learning rate is chosen close to the critical value to access long effective times, but does not report the exact rate, selection rule, training discretization, random seeds, repetitions, uncertainty, or fit window. Width is usually reported as a typical value rather than a full sweep. A near-critical step size can materially affect a discrete trajectory even though the theory is continuous-time gradient flow.

key_findings.claim: The asymptotic regime becomes difficult to observe as dimension grows, weakening practical claims based only on the exponent.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 2 compares d=1,3,6,10 and M=100,1,000,10,000. Its caption explicitly says the spectral index at which the asymptotic starts grows with d; the d=10 curves do not cleanly reach the predicted tail over the available finite spectrum. Density, geometry, and bias enter the coefficient and crossover even when the asymptotic exponent is shared.

key_findings.claim: The rectified-power activation experiment presents half-integer cases as theoretical checks even though the derivation explicitly excludes them.
key_findings.evidence: Section 6.1 and Supplement E derive a degree 2q-1 singularity for phi_q(z)=(z)_+^q except at half-integer q, where a Gamma-function factor diverges and the source says existence of the limiting eigenvalue law must be studied separately. Figure 3 nevertheless plots q=0.5 and q=1.5 with dashed theoretical slopes alongside covered values. Those two curves are empirical extrapolations, not validations of the stated derivation.

key_findings.claim: The depth extension preserves only the local ReLU singularity class; its constants and empirical range are limited.
key_findings.evidence: The recursion argues that fully connected biased ReLU NTKs retain a degree-one diagonal singularity for every depth, hence the same asymptotic slope. Figure 4 covers only d=3 and hidden-layer counts 1-3, and the caption says coefficients C and Lambda were computed only for the shallow case because of complexity. This is not a depth-uniform finite-network theorem and does not cover residual, convolutional, normalized, or attention architectures.

key_findings.claim: The mean-field section does not prove a single fixed power law for the full nonlinear feature-learning trajectory.
key_findings.evidence: The argument linearizes late training around a presumed limiting parameter density and shows that an instantaneous mean-field kernel has a degree-one diagonal singularity when the density is sufficiently smooth and rapidly decaying. But that kernel changes during training. Figure 5 samples kernels at several times for one d=4 GP setup; it does not solve the coupled evolving-kernel dynamics or prove a global asymptotic for arbitrary mean-field training.

key_findings.claim: The Gaussian-process target argument replaces a random realization's norm by its expectation and defers the needed concentration proof.
key_findings.evidence: Supplement D writes ||g_t||^2 approximately equal to its GP expectation before evaluating the asymptotic. Footnote 3 acknowledges that a single realization need not be close when correlations are long, sketches a variance rate based on Wick-Isserlis, and says the proof will be returned to in a subsequent publication. Thus the displayed per-realization GP loss law has an explicit proof gap in this manuscript.

anchors.section: Supplement D / Equations D.13-D.17 and footnote 3

key_findings.claim: The bridge from local Fourier packets to the coefficient-tail law is heuristic rather than a general eigensystem theorem.
key_findings.evidence: Supplement D uses short-time Fourier transforms, local stationary-phase approximations, and approximate localized eigenvectors. It explicitly assumes that suitable discrete wave numbers correspond to approximate eigenvectors in each cell before estimating Q(lambda). These steps motivate the correct-looking exponents but do not establish the coefficient law for every allowed density, boundary, and realization.

key_findings.claim: Supplement D ends with a material exponent typo for the Gaussian scenario.
key_findings.evidence: After deriving Q(lambda) proportional to lambda^(beta/(d+alpha)), the final Scenario 2 summary on page 23 prints kappa=1/d. Algebra and main-text Equation 38 require kappa=beta/d. With the printed value, Theorem 1 would give the discontinuous-target exponent instead of the GP exponent. The surrounding derivation makes the intended correction unambiguous.

key_findings.claim: The smooth-Erf conclusion is only a numerical fit and the plotted tails do not support the full accompanying description.
key_findings.evidence: Supplement F states that the theory does not apply to smooth activations, then fits Erf NTK eigenvalues by an exponential. In Figure 6, several Erf spectra reach a numerical floor around 1e-19 and the coefficient-tail curves visibly plateau, especially in low dimension, even though the text says ReLU and Erf coefficient distributions behave almost identically. The figure cannot establish a true asymptotic exponential or activation-independent eigenvectors.

key_findings.claim: The distribution experiment confirms spectral degeneracy effects but not distribution-independent finite-sample behavior.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 7 compares a spherical Gaussian, a uniform cube, and a random Gaussian mixture. Symmetric distributions produce staircase spectra from degeneracies, while the mixture smooths them. This supports using a nonsymmetric density for visual fits, but also demonstrates that finite-index spectra and crossover structure depend strongly on the distribution even when an asymptotic exponent is claimed to be shared.

key_findings.claim: The empirical package is not reproducible from the paper record.
key_findings.evidence: The experiment description gives typical values such as eight Gaussian components, standard deviation about 0.5, M about 10,000, and width about 3,000, but omits exact draws, seeds, learning rates, fit intervals, slope estimates, error bars, raw spectra, and code. The official arXiv record exposes no author code or data artifact. Visual agreement with dashed lines is therefore not independently auditable as a quantitative fit.

key_findings.claim: One bibliography entry assigns the wrong arXiv identifier to a central spectral-bias paper.
key_findings.evidence: The references list Cao et al., Towards Understanding the Spectral Bias of Deep Learning, as arXiv:1606.05340. The official IJCAI 2021 paper and arXiv record identify it as arXiv:1912.01198; arXiv:1606.05340 is Poole et al., Exponential expressivity in deep neural networks, which the same bibliography also cites separately. This is a source-identity error, not merely a formatting variation.

anchors.section: References / Cao et al. and Poole et al.

key_findings.claim: The paper studies population training-loss decay, not generalization scaling or modern resource scaling laws.
key_findings.evidence: Its dependent variable is expected squared training loss as continuous gradient-flow time grows. It does not derive test error versus sample count, model width, parameter count, or compute, and it has no language-model experiment. Contemporary and later spectrum-dependent learning-curve work addresses those distinct axes. Conflating them would overstate both the target's scope and its relation to neural scaling-law literature.

method.core_idea: Reduce late-time wide-network training to spectral decay under a fixed positive integral operator, then obtain an explicit loss exponent by combining a kernel eigenvalue tail with the initial-error energy tail in the same eigenbasis.
method.mechanism: Linearize full-batch gradient flow around a zero-loss optimum and symmetrize the NTK evolution operator using the square root of the data density. Diagonalize the resulting operator so each mode decays as exp(-lambda_n t). Use singular-integral spectral theory to infer lambda_n from the NTK's diagonal nonsmoothness, and use localized Fourier and stationary-phase arguments to infer coefficient-tail exponents for jump-discontinuous and Gaussian-process initial errors. Combine both exponents through the proved conditional summation theorem. Extend the local singularity calculation to rectified-power activations, deeper biased ReLU networks, and a late-time mean-field kernel.
assumptions: Training is full-batch continuous-time gradient flow on expected quadratic loss with scalar outputs.
The trajectory is close enough to a zero-loss global optimum for first-order output linearization to be valid.
The NTK is fixed during the analyzed dynamics, except for the separately discussed local mean-field snapshot.
The data distribution is a smooth full-dimensional density with compact support or sufficiently rapid decay.
A large empirical sample can be replaced by that continuous population before taking the large-time limit.
The symmetrized evolution operator has a discrete nonnegative spectrum accumulating at zero.
Kernel eigenvalues and initial-error coefficient tails have exact regularly varying power-law asymptotics.
For the ReLU formulas, network biases are nonzero and the diagonal is the only relevant kernel singularity.
The domain boundary and any jump boundary are sufficiently smooth for the local Fourier calculation.
The initial error, not merely the target, belongs to the prescribed discontinuous or Gaussian-process class.
Localized Fourier packets can be associated with approximate eigenvectors densely enough to recover coefficient tails.
For a GP target, a typical realization's squared norm concentrates around its expectation at the stated rate.
For deep ReLU networks, recursive angular singularities retain the same leading degree without cancellation.
For the mean-field extension, the limiting neuron density exists, is smooth, decays rapidly, and supports late-time linearization.

techniques.role: Linearizes output dynamics around a presumed zero-loss optimum.
Conjugates the density-weighted NTK operator into a symmetric integral operator.
Expresses loss as a sum of independently decaying kernel eigenmodes.
Uses the cumulative coefficient energy s_n to absorb local oscillations in individual coefficients.
Derives the loss power law from eigenvalue and coefficient-tail regular variation.
Links a degree-alpha diagonal singularity to eigenvalue exponent 1+alpha/d.
Approximates high-index eigenvectors by localized oscillatory packets.
Computes loss coefficients for jump surfaces and rough Gaussian-process covariance.
Propagates near-diagonal ReLU angular expansions across fully connected layers.
Numerically constructs and eigendecomposes dense infinite-width NTK matrices.
Checks selected trajectories with finite but wide networks and near-critical learning rates.

evaluations.setting: Shallow biased ReLU NTK with d=2 or d=4, random eight-component Gaussian-mixture inputs, and either a ball-indicator or network-GP initial error.
evaluations.metric: Log-log loss trajectory, kernel eigenvalue tail, and coefficient partial-sum tail.
evaluations.result: Figure 1 visually matches predicted slopes xi=1/(d+1) for the indicator and xi=3/(d+1) for the GP over an intermediate range, with finite-spectrum bending at late indices/times.
evaluations.baseline: Dashed analytic asymptotes only; no alternative kernel, non-power fit, quantitative slope estimator, confidence interval, or held-out fit range.

evaluations.setting: Infinite-width shallow ReLU kernels for d=1,3,6,10 and sampled matrix sizes M=100,1,000,10,000.
evaluations.metric: Ordered eigenvalues versus the degree-one singular-kernel approximation and analytic n^(-(1+1/d)) tail.
evaluations.result: Figure 2 shows improved agreement as index and M grow, but the required crossover index grows with dimension and the d=10 tail is not cleanly reached.
evaluations.baseline: The kernel's extracted singular part and predicted asymptote; no finite-sample error rate or formal goodness-of-fit test.

evaluations.setting: Shallow rectified-power kernels phi_q for q=0.5,0.75,1,1.5 in d=1 and d=3.
evaluations.result: Figure 3 visually follows exponent 1+(2q-1)/d, including q=0.5 and 1.5.
evaluations.baseline: Analytic dashed slopes, although the manuscript's derivation explicitly leaves the two plotted half-integer cases unproved.

evaluations.setting: Biased fully connected ReLU NTKs with one to three hidden layers, d=3, and a GP target.
evaluations.result: Figure 4 shows similar slopes across depths, consistent with a degree-one diagonal singularity.
evaluations.baseline: The exact analytic line is computed only for the shallow network; deeper intercepts are not derived and no broader depth or architecture sweep is shown.

evaluations.setting: One mean-field ReLU network on d=4 inputs with a GP target, with kernels measured at initialization and later training times.
evaluations.metric: Training-loss slope and instantaneous-kernel eigenvalue slopes.
evaluations.result: Figure 5 shows an approximately 3/5 loss slope and approximately 5/4 spectral slopes at sampled times.
evaluations.baseline: A fixed theoretical exponent; there is no solution or controlled baseline for the coupled time-dependent kernel dynamics.

evaluations.setting: ReLU versus Erf shallow NTKs with GP targets across d=1-4.
evaluations.result: Figure 6 fits ReLU eigenvalues by a power law and Erf eigenvalues by exponentials, but Erf spectra meet a numerical floor and coefficient tails plateau.
evaluations.baseline: Visual fitted curves only; the text concedes that the theory does not apply to smooth Erf.

evaluations.setting: Spherical Gaussian, uniform-cube, and random Gaussian-mixture input distributions for d=1,3,6,10.
evaluations.result: Figure 7 shows staircase degeneracy under symmetric measures and smoother spectra under the random mixture.
evaluations.baseline: Qualitative distribution comparison without matched uncertainty, finite-M convergence analysis, or loss-trajectory validation.

evaluations.setting: Supplementary analytic derivations for the conditional loss theorem, Fourier coefficients, target classes, activations, depth, and mean field.
evaluations.metric: Internal consistency of stated asymptotic exponents and coefficients.
evaluations.result: The conditional loss theorem is sound, but the target-specific bridge is heuristic, GP concentration is deferred, the Gaussian coefficient summary has a kappa typo, and half-integer activation cases are not proved.
evaluations.baseline: Cross-check against the manuscript's own main equations, assumptions, and plotted cases.

limitations: The exact loss theorem is conditional on two power-law tails; it is not an unconditional neural-network convergence theorem.
The target-specific coefficient-tail derivations use localized approximate eigenvectors and stationary-phase heuristics.
The analysis requires population expected squared loss and a continuous full-dimensional density.
A fixed finite dataset ultimately produces finite-rank exponential decay or a nullspace plateau, not the stated infinite power-law tail.
The kernel is frozen by late-time lazy linearization near a zero-loss optimum.
No theorem covers SGD noise, minibatching, discrete-step stability, momentum, Adam, cross-entropy, label noise, or regularization.
The biased ReLU result does not automatically extend to zero bias, data manifolds, nonsmooth supports, CNNs, transformers, normalization, or residual parameterizations.
Only jump-discontinuous and one Gaussian-process roughness class receive explicit target exponents.
The GP per-realization concentration claim is sketched in a footnote and deferred to future work.
The rectified-power activation proof excludes half-integer q even though two such cases are plotted as theoretical checks.
Smooth-Erf behavior is empirical only and is contaminated by numerical floors.
The deep result derives a shared singularity degree but not coefficients beyond the shallow case.
The mean-field extension studies a late local kernel class, not the full evolving-kernel optimization dynamics.
Experiments are small synthetic regression problems and mostly infinite-width kernel diagonalizations.
There are no exact seeds, learning rates, fit windows, uncertainty estimates, raw results, or public code artifact.
The work analyzes training loss, not test error, sample efficiency, model-size scaling, or compute scaling.
Density and geometry can strongly shift constants, degeneracies, and crossover even if the limiting exponent is invariant.
The official arXiv manuscript remained at v1, so the internal kappa typo and bibliography identity error were never corrected there.
failure_modes: Taking t large at fixed sample size makes the smallest empirical eigenvalue dominate exponentially and invalidates the continuum power-law asymptotic.
High dimension can push the spectral crossover beyond the resolvable range, making a fitted slope a pre-asymptotic artifact.
A smooth or analytic kernel can have super-polynomial eigenvalue decay, so a finite power-law loss exponent need not exist.
Zero bias or a symmetric/discrete input measure can introduce degeneracies or singular sets not covered by the diagonal analysis.
Feature learning changes the NTK and target alignment, invalidating fixed coefficients and fixed eigenvalues.
A nonzero training residual, noise floor, regularization, or kernel nullspace prevents convergence to the claimed zero-loss tail.
A target may be smooth while the actual initial error is not, or vice versa, because random initialization contributes to g.
Near-critical discrete learning rates can create optimizer dynamics absent from the continuous-time model.
Numerical eigendecomposition can hit floating-point floors and produce misleading exponential or plateau fits.
Using half-integer rectified powers invokes cases for which the supplied singular coefficient derivation is explicitly unresolved.
reusable_insights: Separate a rigorous conditional spectral-to-loss theorem from the harder task of proving the spectral premises for a model and target.
State the order of width, data, and time limits whenever an infinite-spectrum power law is compared with a finite experiment.
Track both kernel eigenvalues and target energy in the eigenbasis; either alone is insufficient to predict loss decay.
Use cumulative coefficient tails rather than individual coefficients when local oscillations obscure regular variation.
Treat the diagonal singularity degree as a useful universality-class descriptor, while measuring the coefficient and crossover separately.
Distinguish initial-error regularity from target regularity because initialization and density weighting alter the relevant function.
Validate asymptotic slopes with expanding sample sizes, preregistered fit windows, confidence intervals, and explicit crossover diagnostics.
For feature-learning regimes, model the coupled evolution of kernels and target alignment rather than freezing an instantaneous spectrum.
Use analytic smooth activations as a falsification boundary for any blanket power-law spectral claim.
Audit figures against theorem exclusions: visually matching a predicted line does not convert an excluded case into a proved one.
open_questions: Can the localized Fourier-packet arguments for the two target classes be replaced by rigorous coefficient-tail theorems on general domains?
What finite-M, finite-width, and finite-time error bounds quantify the window in which the continuum power law is observable?
How does the crossover scale grow with dimension, data geometry, density minima, and bias magnitude?
What is the correct asymptotic at half-integer rectified powers and for analytic activations such as Erf or tanh?
Can one prove concentration of the GP loss for individual long-correlated realizations under explicit covariance assumptions?
How do SGD noise, learning-rate schedules, momentum, and adaptive optimizers alter the spectral time exponent?
Which exponent survives when the NTK evolves through feature learning or edge-of-stability training?
Can analogous singularity classes be derived for convolutional, residual, attention, and normalized architectures?
How should training-loss time laws be connected, if at all, to generalization versus data, width, and compute?
Can an open benchmark release exact kernels, targets, fits, seeds, and code so competing spectral and non-spectral explanations can be compared quantitatively?

competitive_landscape.title: Neural Tangent Kernel: Convergence and Generalization in Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: Foundational predecessor introducing the infinite-width frozen-NTK gradient-flow description.
competitive_landscape.difference: It establishes kernel dynamics and generalization properties; the target derives a particular large-time population-loss exponent from spectral tails.

competitive_landscape.title: The Convergence Rate of Neural Networks for Learned Functions of Different Frequencies
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct spectral-learning antecedent for frequency-dependent convergence in shallow ReLU NTKs.
competitive_landscape.difference: It uses spherical symmetry and harmonic modes; the target moves to nonsymmetric smooth densities and aggregates modes into total time-loss exponents.

competitive_landscape.title: On the Inductive Bias of Neural Tangent Kernels
competitive_landscape.relationship: Predecessor analyzing NTK smoothness, RKHS approximation, and spectral inductive bias.
competitive_landscape.difference: It characterizes function-space bias rather than deriving the target's explicit late-time loss asymptotic.

competitive_landscape.title: On the Similarity between the Laplace and Neural Tangent Kernels
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct predecessor for polynomial ReLU-NTK eigenvalue decay and RKHS equivalence on the sphere.
competitive_landscape.difference: The target broadens the geometry to general smooth densities and combines eigendecay with target coefficients to predict optimization time.

competitive_landscape.title: Deep Equals Shallow for ReLU Networks in Kernel Regimes
competitive_landscape.relationship: Very close predecessor showing that deep and shallow fully connected ReLU kernels share approximation and eigendecay properties.
competitive_landscape.difference: It works on the sphere and focuses approximation; the target emphasizes general-domain local singularities and late-time loss, but its depth novelty is narrower than the title suggests.

competitive_landscape.title: A Spectral Analysis of Dot-product Kernels
competitive_landscape.relationship: Competing smoothness analysis covering polynomial, geometric, and super-geometric eigendecay regimes.
competitive_landscape.difference: It demonstrates that analytic smoothness can yield faster-than-power spectra, delimiting the target's rectified-power universality class.

competitive_landscape.title: Spectrum Dependent Learning Curves in Kernel Regression and Wide Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct antecedent linking kernel spectra and target coefficients to learning curves.
competitive_landscape.difference: Its independent variable is training-sample count and its outcome is generalization error; the target studies population training loss versus gradient-flow time.

competitive_landscape.title: Asymptotic learning curves of kernel methods: empirical data v.s. Teacher-Student paradigm
competitive_landscape.relationship: Predecessor deriving sample-size error exponents from target smoothness and kernel spectral coefficients.
competitive_landscape.difference: It concerns generalization versus sample size, while the target isolates deterministic optimization-time decay in a population operator.

competitive_landscape.title: Spectral Bias and Task-Model Alignment Explain Generalization in Kernel Regression and Infinitely Wide Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: Contemporary competitor relating kernel eigensystems and target alignment to generalization.
competitive_landscape.difference: It derives finite-sample generalization behavior for broad kernels and distributions rather than the target's large-time training-loss tail.

competitive_landscape.title: Explaining Neural Scaling Laws
competitive_landscape.relationship: Contemporaneous spectrum-based theory for data-, model-, and resolution-limited neural scaling laws.
competitive_landscape.difference: It uses resource and generalization scaling, clarifying that the target's use of scaling laws refers to a different axis: population loss versus time.

competitive_landscape.title: Deep learning versus kernel learning: an empirical study of loss landscape geometry and the time evolution of the Neural Tangent Kernel
competitive_landscape.relationship: Empirical counterpoint showing substantial early NTK evolution and feature learning in practical finite networks.
competitive_landscape.difference: It studies realistic evolving kernels, limiting extension of the target's frozen-kernel asymptotic to the full training trajectory.

competitive_landscape.title: Feature Learning in Infinite-Width Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: Alternative infinite-width theory distinguishing kernel and feature-learning parameterizations.
competitive_landscape.difference: It shows that infinite width need not imply a static NTK; the target analyzes the kernel regime and a much more local mean-field extension.

competitive_landscape.title: A Theory of Neural Tangent Kernel Alignment and Its Influence on Training
competitive_landscape.relationship: Close contemporaneous successor modeling feature-driven kernel alignment during training.
competitive_landscape.difference: It separates an early feature-learning phase from later kernel-like power-law behavior, whereas the target freezes the operator in its main result.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning Curves for SGD on Structured Features
competitive_landscape.relationship: Closest early successor deriving stochastic learning dynamics from feature spectra.
competitive_landscape.difference: It incorporates SGD, minibatches, and finite or fresh datasets, but remains in a lazy structured-feature regime rather than proving the target's singular-kernel geometry.

competitive_landscape.title: Self-Consistent Dynamical Field Theory of Kernel Evolution in Wide Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: Successor solving coupled time-dependent kernels in infinite-width feature-learning networks.
competitive_landscape.difference: It treats evolving-kernel dynamics that the target's mean-field singularity snapshot does not solve and shows static-NTK approximations can fail.

competitive_landscape.title: On the Eigenvalue Decay Rates of a Class of Neural-Network Related Kernel Functions Defined on General Domains
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct rigorous successor for eigenvalue decay on general domains across depths and activations.
competitive_landscape.difference: It systematizes and strengthens the general-domain eigendecay component and connects it to minimax generalization; the target additionally connects a target tail to time-loss decay.

competitive_landscape.title: How Feature Learning Can Improve Neural Scaling Laws
competitive_landscape.relationship: Strong modern successor deriving beyond-kernel scaling across time, model size, and data.
competitive_landscape.difference: It shows feature learning can change time and compute exponents for hard targets outside the initial NTK RKHS, directly limiting frozen-NTK universality.

competitive_landscape.title: Functional Scaling Laws in Kernel Regression: Loss Dynamics and Learning Rate Schedules
competitive_landscape.relationship: Current successor studying full power-law kernel-regression loss dynamics under one-pass SGD and arbitrary learning-rate schedules.
competitive_landscape.difference: It adds stochasticity, intrinsic time, data/compute limits, schedule dependence, and LLM loss-curve experiments beyond the target's fixed-rate population gradient flow.

competitive_landscape.title: Dynamics of neural scaling laws in random feature regression with powerlaw-distributed kernel eigenvalues
competitive_landscape.relationship: Current dynamical mean-field successor unifying gradient flow, weight decay, Langevin dynamics, and generalization under power-law spectra.
competitive_landscape.difference: It studies typical high-dimensional random-feature generalization and early stopping under multiple dynamics; the target derives geometry-specific population training-loss exponents.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Large-time neural-network training loss follows an explicit universal power law whose exponent depends only on input dimension, activation smoothness, and target-function class; this holds for shallow and deep NTK networks and extends to mean-field training.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper proves a clean conditional eigenvalue-and-coefficient-tail theorem, imports singular-integral asymptotics to obtain ReLU NTK eigenvalue decay on nonsymmetric smooth densities, derives explicit jump and GP loss exponents with local Fourier arguments, and shows qualitative agreement in synthetic kernel and selected wide-network experiments.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The defensible novelty is a useful synthesis: an explicit population training-time loss asymptotic that combines a general-domain kernel singularity with target roughness, including coefficients for two classes. The broad spectral-bias premise, ReLU eigendecay, depth equivalence, and spectrum-dependent scaling substantially predate it. The strongest universality language does not survive close scope audit because fixed finite data are ultimately exponential, target-tail derivations are partly heuristic, the GP concentration proof is deferred, half-integer cases are plotted despite exclusion, and practical networks often evolve their kernels. Later general-domain eigendecay, SGD dynamics, learning-rate-schedule, and feature-learning theories materially narrow the remaining novelty.

reviewer_notes: Read all 29 pages of the canonical arXiv v1 PDF and exact cached text, including the full 18-page supplement; visually inspected every rendered page at original resolution and every panel/caption in Figures 1-7. Audited Equations 2-42, Supplementary Theorem 1 and its proof, the Fourier-transform coefficient calculation, both target-class derivations, activation/depth/mean-field extensions, and all reference pages. No figure pixels were unavailable. Confirmed the page-23 Gaussian-scenario kappa typo against main Equation 38 and the derivation; confirmed that Figure 3 plots both excluded half-integer q cases; confirmed the Erf numerical floors and low-dimensional coefficient plateaus visually. The official arXiv record has only v1 (submitted 2021-05-02) and exposes no author code/data artifact. The Cao et al. bibliography identifier was checked against the official IJCAI 2021 record and arXiv:1912.01198. Independently checked 19 primary-paper predecessors, direct competitors, and successors through 2026-08-23, with special attention to spectral bias, general-domain eigendecay, finite-data SGD, evolving NTKs, feature learning, and modern functional scaling laws.
